One design for the first version: one optional backup host. Nothing here was built or run; every name taken from the roles plan, K1, G1/G2 and E1 is plan text, and the code was read at dd223af.

The design in ten sentences. (1) The host names a backup with one governance record, `BackupSet { backup }`; removing that member clears the name; nothing asks for it and `goal status` says `Backup host: none` as a fact. (2) A change of host is one record, `HostChanged { base, host, endorsement }`, at position 0 of a new governance key's log; `base` is any record of the old key's log (K1 put the host's steps in that log, so one cutoff covers members, rules and recordings). (3) The new key is computed from the backup agent's seed, the goal and the base, and the record carries no clock reading, so taking over twice from the same base is the same bytes, and a new host restored from any copy computes its key again. (4) The record counts only if the member it names is the backup at the base; it is void if the old key signed, at a position after the base, a removal of that member or a `BackupSet` naming anyone else or nobody (the owner's answer 18), and void if its own key later signed `TakeoverWithdrawn`. (5) One live record on a term is in force; two or more dispute the term and halt membership and rules until all but one are withdrawn, which the same person can always do because every one of their keys is computable from their agent's seed. (6) Whatever the old key signed outside the base's ancestry is set aside whenever it arrives, work built on it is excluded and never pending, and the author's next record on the kept chain counts. (7) The takeover record itself opens a new content key epoch, and keys are stored and requested by the record that opened them. (8) The new host's computer repeats, by itself, any removal the old host had signed that it receives later; the old host sees which of its changes the backup has received. (9) The change, or the record that voids it, is pushed once on the fork-proof route to every computer ever admitted that is no longer a member; the old host stays a member, its invitations and page do not move, and it can be handed the goal back. (10) A planned handoff is the same record: the giver names the other person and goes quiet, the other person takes over.

What it costs: the chain builder is rewritten around terms (by judgement 2,500 to 3,500 production lines and about 4,000 of tests for B1, 900 to 1,300 and 1,500 for B2; not measured); three new record kinds; one changed sync request and one new frame; protocol, API and store go to 8 and goals made before do not load. A takeover is not final until the old host's computer is heard from or is truly gone. A removal that only the lost computer held is lost and reopens reading. A dispute between two different backups needs the loser to withdraw.

Three phases: B1 (naming, taking over, the whole replay rule, protocol 8), B2 (everyone is told, handing over, the old host's removals), B3 (qualification and release). Two small models are written first.
draft.user_explanation: A host can name one member as backup host; nothing asks for this, and a goal without one keeps working until its host's computer is lost. The backup host's owner can take over at any time with one command, alone and without the host's yes, because a lost computer and a sleeping one look the same from outside. From then on their computer keeps who is in and the rules, and whatever the old host's computer had signed that the backup's had not yet received is dropped even if it shows up later: someone it admitted joins again, and a removal it made is repeated by the new host's computer when it arrives. A host who was only asleep wakes up as an ordinary member: they keep their work and their copy, their invitations and public page stop working, and the new host can hand the goal back. One thing of the old host's always wins: if they had removed the backup host or named a different one, the takeover and everything done under it is dropped when that record arrives. Goals made before this version of Locust do not continue under it.

choices.problem: Who picks the base, and how a renamed or removed backup is stopped (research section 7, first problem; items 1 and 4)
choices.chosen: The taker's daemon picks the base: the last record of the old governance key it holds with everything before it. Validity is a pure function of the held set. A change record is authorized when the member it names is the backup in the snapshot at the base. It is revoked when the held set contains any record of the old key at a position after the base that removes that member or is a `BackupSet` naming anyone else or nobody. Removing a member clears the name in the same step, so a removed backup is never a backup at a later base. Before signing, the daemon must have heard from one other computer; a backup that was removed is refused by every member that holds the removal, so it cannot meet that rule without `--alone`.
choices.cost: A takeover that every computer treated as in force is undone when the old host's record surfaces, with every later change of host built on it. That can be days later, until the old host's computer next syncs or is known gone. Revocation is judged by position in the old key's log, not by descent, so on an old log that was forked by a restore the outcome follows whichever copy signed the later position.
choices.rejected: The takeover stands (the owner decided the removal wins). Read the backup only at the base and ignore later records (a stale copy of any once-named key acts for ever; the first break of the successor design). Refuse to remove a member while it is named (the host could not remove a hostile backup in one step, and un-naming has the same race). Old electors acknowledge a change of backup, or a second signature on governance (the owner set both aside). Revocation by `prev` descent from the base (a removed taker would need the whole log segment to check it; by position one record proves it, so it can be told on the fork-proof route).

choices.problem: How the new governance key is made (item 3)
choices.chosen: Derived: seed = BLAKE3 derive_key("locust v8 governance key", agent seed, goal, base position, base id). The content key the record opens is derived from that seed. The record's `at_ms` is 0. Sealing is deterministic in today's code (seal.rs) and so is an Ed25519 signature, so the same agent taking over from the same base signs the same bytes on any copy of its data.
choices.cost: The governance key of a later term is as strong as its host agent's seed and no stronger; both sit in the same data folder with no passphrase. The record carries no time, so others show when they received it. After a withdrawal the same base can never be used again by that agent.
choices.rejected: A fresh random key: a backup restored from a copy older than its takeover has lost the key for good, so the goal has a host on paper and nobody who can sign; and every repeated takeover is a second, different record. Deriving without the base: two takeovers from different bases would be two records at position 0 of one log, a fork inside the new term that the ordinary rule cannot read.

choices.problem: A dispute that must not be permanent (research section 7, second problem; item 5)
choices.chosen: Same base gives one record, so the common case is no dispute. Two different live change records on one term dispute it: the chain stops at the part of the old log both keep, nobody signs governance, members' work at kept anchors goes on. It ends when all but one are void. The signer of a change record can void it with `TakeoverWithdrawn`, signed by that record's own key after it. One person's takeovers all come from one agent seed, so that person can always withdraw their own from any copy. The guard's marks tell a restored backup that it signed as host here before.
choices.cost: One more record kind. Membership and rules are halted until a person runs one command that status prints. Between two different backups (possible only when the old host's own log was forked and named one on each side) the one who gives way must act; if that person is gone the halt stays. Withdrawing the only live record hands the chain back to the old key; the daemon never does that.
choices.rejected: The earlier base wins (a late record voids a settled week, silently). The deeper base wins (an honest stale copy flips a settled change). A new takeover that lists the ones it supersedes (it drops both terms' work, and a third copy disputes it again). Permanent halt (the requirement). Ordering by the endorser's own agent log (a restored backup has usually forked that log, so its endorsements would wait for ever).

choices.problem: Removals a takeover has not seen (research section 7, third problem; item 6)
choices.chosen: Four parts. Before signing, the backup's daemon asks every other computer and continues from the union of what they hold. The host is told what its backup holds: after each completed exchange with the backup's computer the host's daemon notes its own log tip, and `goal status` and the result of `member remove` say when a removal has not reached the backup. After a takeover, when the new host's daemon holds a set-aside removal signed by a key of an earlier term on its chain, and the member is still in under that same admission, it signs the same removal itself, with the same cutoff, unasked. The takeover record opens a new content key, so nobody writes under a key the removed member was the last to get.
choices.cost: A removal that only the lost computer held never arrives: that member is in again and reads everything, and nobody is told. A host that has been replaced and has not learned it can still remove members, and the new host's computer repeats those removals. One local record on the host's daemon.
choices.rejected: A removal is final only once acknowledged (a second signature; the owner set it aside). Refuse a takeover until every member is reached or named to skip (a goal with many members asleep would ask for a list). Offer the removal to the new host under Waiting for you (reading stays open until a person acts, and it is a prompt). Derive what the backup has seen from the anchors of its agent's records only (it lags by however long that agent is silent, and an agent at level read never signs).

choices.problem: The cutoff being any record of the old signer; what a takeover sets aside (research section 7, fourth problem; item 11)
choices.chosen: `base` is an `AuthorPoint` in the old governance key's log and may be a host step. The record's anchor is the last governance record at or before it. Set aside is every record of the old key not reached from the base by `prev`, by position in that one log. A host step counts only if its signer is the governance key of the term its anchor is in and the step is in that key's kept log. A set-aside decision holds no place after its predecessor. The new host signs nothing but the takeover record: no forced rules binding and no new tree epoch.
choices.cost: A plan text recorded after the base is recorded again by itself, because a revision builds on a revision. A file change that built on a set-aside acceptance names that acceptance as its parent, so it is rebuilt and approved again. A task opened by a set-aside stage step is opened again as a new round and work on the old round is lost. `resolve`, the stage runner, the first-files test and the task creator read the term at an anchor.
choices.rejected: The base must be a governance record (every recording since the last admission is lost at every takeover). A second cutoff for the host agent's key (K1 already put host steps in the governance log). A mandatory rules binding and tree epoch as the new host's first acts (they were asked for to close streams with two authorities; once set-aside records are excluded before the successor check they close nothing, and they would make every open revision and proposal be posted again).

choices.problem: Telling the deposed host and whoever it admitted afterwards (research section 7, fifth problem; item 8)
choices.chosen: The old host's agent stays a member, so ordinary sync reaches it until the new host removes it. For everyone ordinary sync does not reach, one record is pushed on the fork-proof route, once per computer: the change record when a change is in force, or the record that voided it. It goes to every endpoint named in any held admission that is not bound to a current member. The receiver keeps it only if it passes the full validity rule against what it holds; a computer the old host admitted after the base holds the whole old log, so one record is enough. A computer none of whose agents is a member or joining stops dialing.
choices.cost: One new frame and one delivered record per computer. A computer that missed two changes learns only the first, which is enough to stop it. A computer that is off learns nothing until it is on. A removed member that the change does not concern is still never told of its removal.
choices.rejected: Serve the governance keys' whole logs to every computer ever admitted (a removed member would learn the names, keys and endpoints of everyone admitted after it left). Refuse to remove the previous host until the notice reached it (a lost computer never acknowledges, so the new host could never remove it). A proof frame that carries ancestry (not needed for one backup: the receiver already holds the kept log).

choices.problem: Catching up before signing after a restore (research section 7, sixth problem; item 3)
choices.chosen: The restore guard as G1 builds it, with three uses. The takeover command refuses while `Node::hold` holds the backup agent's key. It also refuses when the marks name, in this goal, a key the store does not hold: this computer signed as host here before. When a daemon holds a change record that names one of its agents and lacks the key, it computes the key again and the guard holds it until that key's records are back. That an old host has been replaced is not a hold: `Goal::next` answers nothing for a key that is not the last term's.
choices.cost: After a whole-computer restore with nobody reachable, a person who runs both overrides (`goal continue`, then `goal takeover --alone`) can still take over a second time from another base; that is the dispute. A wake from sleep still costs nothing, so a host that was asleep can sign a few records before its first exchange.
choices.rejected: A timer that delays signing (it only delays; the rule against clocks is about agreement, but G1 already chose that a wake costs nothing). One exchange before the first unattended signature after a wake (left out; it narrows a window that the set-aside rule already makes safe).

choices.problem: Content keys across two signers; a fresh key after a takeover (research section 7, seventh problem; item 7)
choices.chosen: Keys are stored by the id of the record that opened them (first record, removal, or change of host), and `KeyRequest` and `Key` name that record. `HostChanged` opens an epoch like a removal: its payload is sealed under a key derived from the new governance seed, the epoch is one more than at its anchor, and every active member may read it. Keys opened by set-aside records stay where they are held, readable there, and are neither asked for nor served.
choices.cost: Two sync frames and the key store's layout change. Every takeover costs one epoch. Rules whose text was sealed under a key only the old host held cannot be read by anyone; the plan says so and the new host binds rules again.
choices.rejected: Drop a set-aside epoch's key (the authors lose their own text; signing commits only the sealed blob). Keep the bare epoch number on the wire (after an undo two keys share a number and a computer cannot ask for the one it needs). A standalone rotation record (a third way to open an epoch; nothing else needs it in this version).

choices.problem: Public page, door and invitations (research section 7, eighth problem; item 10)
choices.chosen: Nothing moves. Invitation records, the door record and the page's upload seed are on the old host's disk and stay there. A change of host clears the publication on the chain. A ticket gains `issuer`, the key that signed it, beside the goal's first key. The old host's daemon, on learning it was replaced, revokes its pending invitations and blanks its page; it can still delete the page. The new host invites, opens a door and publishes again; the takeover plan says so.
choices.cost: A new address; every member consents again; the gallery listing and the alias are asked for again. The page of a host that is truly gone keeps its last content, with a Join band that reaches nobody, until the farm service expires it.
choices.rejected: Derive the upload seed from the governance key (that key does not move either, and whoever holds a governance key would hold the page). Carry the seed in a bundle with the backup (a copy of a secret that only one computer should hold). Let the farm service move a page to a new key from the signed chain (sound, but the service would have to read the chain; a later step).

choices.problem: The planned handoff (research sections 6 and 8; item 2)
choices.chosen: The same record and the same rule. `goal give` names the other member as backup if they are not, and puts a third reason into the guard's hold, `Giving`, so the giver's governance key signs nothing until the other person takes over or the giver runs `goal keep`. The other person runs `goal takeover`. Nothing is dropped, because nothing was signed after the base.
choices.cost: Two more commands and one local record. If the other person never acts, the goal admits nobody and records nothing until `goal keep`.
choices.rejected: A handoff record in the old host's log (a restored old host that signs at that position forks the log; the electors design broke there). The old host's signature as the approval inside the change record (the two computers would have to exchange a key before signing, and it is a second way for a change to be valid). No quiet at all (an admission in the second between the taker's last exchange and the host's receipt would be dropped).

choices.problem: The dedicated signing key across terms (research section 7, ninth problem; items 13 and the three plugs)
choices.chosen: K1 gives each goal a governance key. This design makes the key a function of the chain: `Chain::build` walks terms, and a snapshot carries the governance key, the host's agent and the backup of its term. K1's two replay rules read the term: an admission of any governance key is excluded, and a removal of the host's agent of the current term is excluded. After a change the old host's agent is an ordinary member and can be removed. A role list whose only holder was the old host's agent passes to the new host's agent.
choices.cost: The chain builder is rewritten, and the eleven tests that pin today's fork behaviour are rewritten with it. Each term and each rejected change record adds one author to every frontier, which holds at most 4,096.
choices.rejected: Copying the key to another computer (the Move the key design: the set of holders only grows and a stale holder voids live governance). Keeping roles with a lost host's agent (a goal under `directed` would have nobody who can pick or close until the new host ran one command per role).

draft.phases_markdown:
### B1: A backup host, and taking over

**Goal.** A host can name one member as backup host, name another, or clear the name. The backup host's owner can take over with one command, alone. From then on their computer signs who is in, the rules and the host's steps with a new governance key. Every computer sets aside what the old key signed that the backup's computer had not received, whenever it arrives. One thing of the old host's wins over a takeover: a removal of the backup, or a record that names another backup or none. Naming is optional and nothing asks for it. This phase takes protocol 8, and no goal made before it loads.

**Depends on.** The whole build order through R10 and the first public release. By name: K1 (`State.governance`, `State.host`, `Local.governance`, `Node::key_for`, `Node::hosts`, `Body::host_may_sign`, the record `K`); G1 and G2 (`Node::hold`, `Hold`, `Node::guard_sources`, `Node::heard`, `Host::reconciled`, the marks, `Why::ThisComputer`); E1 (`Body::GoalEnded`, `Exclusion::AfterEnd`, `State.ended`, `Chain.cut_end`, `ENDED`, the comment `PLUG host-replacement`); R2 (`cli/confirm.rs`, `cli/only_you.rs`); R3 (`Refused`, `Why`, `Act`); R4 (member names, role lists, `resolve` with an anchor, the only-member part, the first-files rule); R5 (the status view, `WaitingKind`); R8 and R9 (`ScopeDecided` signed by the governance key, `desired_selections`). All of these are plan text, not code. The two models named under "Model first" are written and run before `chain.rs` is touched. Nothing is released between B1 and B3.

**Changes.** Terms, each with one meaning below.

- A *term* is the part of a goal's history signed by one governance key. Term 0 is signed by the key the first record names.
- The *backup host* is the member the latest `BackupSet` in force names. Removing that member clears it. A change of host clears it.
- A *change record* is `HostChanged`. It starts the next term. Its *base* is the record of the previous term's key that it names. That key's *kept log* is the base and everything before it in that key's log, following `prev`.
- A change record is *placed* when the base and the whole kept log are held and the kept log's governance records form a chain. It is *authorized* when the member it names is the backup host in the snapshot at its anchor. It is *revoked* when the held set contains a record of the previous term's key, at a position after the base, that removes that member or is a `BackupSet` naming anyone else or nobody. It is *withdrawn* when its own key signed a `TakeoverWithdrawn` reached from that record back to it by `prev`. Placed, authorized, not revoked, not withdrawn and with no end in its kept log is *live*.
- A term with exactly one live change record: that record is *in force*. With two or more the term is *disputed*. With none the term is the last.
- A record is *set aside* when a governance key signed it and it is not on the chain: a record of a term's key outside its kept log, or any record of a change record's key while that change is not in force or is built on one that is not.

Every one of these is a function of the signed events held. No clock, arrival order or identifier comparison enters.

- [lib.rs](../crates/locust-proto/src/lib.rs): `PROTOCOL_VERSION` and `API_VERSION` 7 to 8. [schema.rs](../crates/locust-store/src/schema.rs): `VERSION` 7 to 8. [site.json](site.json) follows. The refusal a store of marker 7 gets is text B-9.
- [event.rs](../crates/locust-proto/src/event.rs): three last variants, all governance. `Body::BackupSet { backup: Option<PublicKey> }` (index 27, `backup_set`). `Body::HostChanged { base: AuthorPoint, host: PublicKey, endorsement: Signature }` (index 28, `host_changed`). `Body::TakeoverWithdrawn` (index 29, `takeover_withdrawn`, no fields). `Header::check`: a `HostChanged` has `seq` 0, a payload, `host` different from its author, and an `endorsement` that verifies under `host` over the digest of (goal, base, author, host) in the new domain `HOST_CHANGE_SIGNATURE`; a `BackupSet` and a `TakeoverWithdrawn` carry no payload; a `TakeoverWithdrawn` has `seq` above 0. `dependencies()` of `HostChanged` is the base's id.
- [crypto.rs](../crates/locust-proto/src/crypto.rs): `Keypair::governance_for(agent: &Keypair, goal: GoalId, base: AuthorPoint) -> Keypair`, whose seed is `derive_key("locust v8 governance key", agent seed, goal, base.seq, base.id)`, and `ContentKey::opened_by_change(governance: &Keypair) -> ContentKey`. Both are frozen in [vectors.rs](../crates/locust-proto/src/vectors.rs).
- [invite.rs](../crates/locust-proto/src/invite.rs): `Invitation` gains `issuer: PublicKey` after `governance`, in the signing digest; the ticket is signed by `issuer`. `governance` stays the goal's first key.
- [sync.rs](../crates/locust-proto/src/sync.rs): `KeyRequest { opened_by: EventId }` and `Key { opened_by, key }` replace the epoch number. The module text says a key is named by the record that opened it.
- [standing.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/goal/standing.rs): `Exclusion` gains `SetAside`, `Revoked`, `Withdrawn`, `NotBackup` and `Unplaced`. `Halt` gains `HostDispute { changes: Vec<EventId> }`. A disputed change record has the existing `Standing::Disputed`. No change record is ever `Pending`.
- [state.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/goal/state.rs): `State` gains `backup: Option<PublicKey>` and `terms: Vec<Term { governance, host, change: Option<EventId>, base: Option<AuthorPoint> }>`; `governance` and `host` are the last term's.
- [history.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/goal/history.rs): `History::kept(point) -> Option<&[Slot]>`, the `prev` walk from a point to position 0, cached; none when a link is not held.
- [chain.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/goal/chain.rs): `Snapshot` gains `governance`, `host`, `backup` and `key: EventId` (the record that opened the current content key). The loop body of `Chain::build` becomes `step(snapshot, event) -> Standing`, and `build` becomes a walk over terms:
  1. Start at the first key with an empty snapshot.
  2. Collect the held change records whose base is in this key's log. For each, test placed, then `anchor` equal to the last governance record of the kept log, then authorized (`step` folded along the kept log gives the snapshot), then the payload epoch (one more than at the anchor). A failure is `Unplaced`, `Unplaced`, `NotBackup` or `BadEpoch`. One whose kept log holds an effective `GoalEnded` is `AfterEnd`. This is the place E1 marked `PLUG host-replacement`.
  3. Mark revoked and withdrawn ones `Revoked` and `Withdrawn`.
  4. None live: this is the last term. Fold its usable prefix as today; a fork is `Halt::Fork`; E1's `cut_end` reads this key's log only.
  5. One live: fold the governance records of its kept log, then the change record. It takes the next position. Its snapshot has `governance` its author, `host` its `host`, no backup, no publication, the epoch plus one, `key` its own id, and every role list whose only holder was the old host's agent holds the new one. Go to 2 with its author.
  6. Two or more live: fold the governance records that every one of their kept logs holds, set `Halt::HostDispute`, stop.
  `step` gains three arms. `BackupSet`: with a member, it must be a current member, not the term's host's agent, and bound to another endpoint than the host's agent, else `Precondition`; it sets `snapshot.backup`. `MemberRemoved` also clears `backup` when it removes that member. K1's two rules read the term: an admission of any held governance key is excluded, and a removal of `snapshot.host` is excluded.
  `authorize_base`: a governance record with no standing from the walk is `SetAside` when its author is a governance key of any term or held change record, `NotAdministrator`'s successor otherwise. A record that is not governance, signed by a governance key, is effective only when `snapshot(anchor).governance` is its author and it is in that key's kept log (the usable prefix for the last term); else `SetAside`. For every other author: an anchor that is held and set aside gives `Excluded(SetAside)`; in the walk back along the author's log an ancestor whose anchor is set aside is skipped, it neither makes the record pending nor counts for `AnchorRegressed`. So work built on set-aside records is excluded, and the author's next record at a kept anchor is judged normally.
- [fold.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/goal/fold.rs), [rules.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/goal/rules.rs), [goal/flow.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/goal/flow.rs): wherever R4, R8, R9 and K1 read `State.governance` or `State.host` for a judged record, they read `snapshot(anchor)`: the authority of an agreed document and of the shared files, the stage runner, the first-files author. A stage task whose opening step a governance key signed has, as its creator, the governance key of the term at the judged record's anchor. In `Verifier::new` the decision index uses one stand-in author for every governance key, so two host decisions after one predecessor dispute that scope. `desired_selections` ignores set-aside decisions when it asks whether a host decision follows `previous`.
- [goal/mod.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/goal/mod.rs): `Goal::next` answers nothing for a governance key that is not the last term's, and for every governance key under `HostDispute`. New `Goal::takeover_base(&self) -> Option<AuthorPoint>`: the tip of the last term's usable prefix.
- [screen.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/goal/screen.rs): kept are records by any governance key of a held term or held change record, by any key such a key admitted, and a `HostChanged` whose base is held or in the batch and whose `host` some held `BackupSet` names. A `HostChanged` that a held record already revokes is dropped.
- [node/local.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/node/local.rs): K1's record `K` is keyed by goal and public key; `Local.governance` becomes a map. New record `T` (goal): the change this daemon signed and when.
- [entry.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/node/entry.rs) and [replica.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/node/replica.rs): `Space::Key` is keyed by goal and opening record and holds the epoch number and the key. Sealing uses `snapshot(head).key`. Reading tries the keys held for the blob's epoch number. `key`, `wanted_keys` and `offer_key` take the opening record; `offer_key` accepts a `HostChanged` as proof like a removal; keys of set-aside records are not wanted and not served.
- `crates/locust-core/src/node/requests/hosts.rs` (new) and [api.rs](../crates/locust-proto/src/api.rs):
  - `backup.set { goal, backup: Option<PublicKey>, expected }` (goal-scoped, `Host`, not a tool): `host()`, then the checks of `step`, then one `BackupSet`.
  - `takeover.plan { goal }` (`Owner`, read only): marks every pair of the goal due through new `Node::reach(goal)`, which also empties the goal's entry in `Guard::heard`, and answers `TakeoverPlan { base, anchor, host_name, host_last_sync_ms, heard, unreached, refused, sole_roles, rules_readable, published, conflict }`.
  - `goal.takeover { goal, agent, base, alone }` (`Owner`, not a tool). In order: the goal holds an end, `conflict(ENDED)`; `agent` is local, active, has not left and is `state().backup`, else `denied("only the backup host takes over")`; `hold(entry, agent)` answers a reason, or the marks name in this goal a key the store does not hold, then G2's `read_only`; `base` is not `takeover_base()`, `conflict("the plan changed")`; `heard(goal)` holds no computer other than the host's while one exists and `alone` is false, `unavailable`. Then it derives the key, signs `HostChanged` at position 0 with `at_ms` 0 through `sign_at`, and writes `K`, the content key and `T` in the same commit. Signing the same record again answers it.

### B2: Everyone is told, handing over, and the old host's removals

**Goal.** A computer that a change of host drops, or that took over in vain, learns it from one pushed record and stops. A host that was replaced sees what was dropped and what it can do. A host sees which of its changes its backup has received. The new host's computer repeats a removal the old host had signed when it receives it. A host hands a goal over with one command and nothing is dropped.

**Depends on.** B1. G1 (`Hold`, `Host::reconciled`, `revoke_pending`). E1 (the delete-only path of `FarmOff`). R5.

**Changes.** A *notice* is one signed record sent on the evidence exchange that today carries a fork proof.
- [sync.rs](../crates/locust-proto/src/sync.rs): last variant `SyncMessage::Notice(WireEvent)`. The evidence exchange is `Hello`, then `HaltProof` or `Notice`, then `Done`.
- [driver.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/sync/driver.rs) and [responder.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/sync/responder.rs): `Host::halt_proofs` becomes `Host::evidence() -> Vec<(GoalId, EndpointId, Evidence)>` with `Evidence::{Fork([WireEvent; 2]), Notice(WireEvent)}`; `Dialed.proof` carries either. The responder hands a `Notice` to new `Host::receive_notice`.
- [peers.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/node/peers.rs): `evidence()` adds, for each change record in force, that record; and for each held change record that is `Revoked` or `Withdrawn`, the lowest-positioned record that voided it. Each goes to every endpoint named in a held admission by any governance key that is not bound to a current member and is not this daemon, until new local record `n` (goal, endpoint, event) says it was delivered. `receive_notice` accepts from a historical contact; it keeps a `HostChanged` that passes `screen`, and a removal, `BackupSet` or `TakeoverWithdrawn` by a governance key it knows that voids a change record it holds; anything else is dropped without a refusal. `peers()` lists nothing for a goal in which no local agent is a member or joining.
- [commit.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/node/commit.rs), in `advance`, when the last term's key changes and this daemon holds the key of an earlier term: `revoke_pending` for the goal; clear `Hold::Giving`; write local record `p` (goal) with the change's id, so status can say it once.
- [node/farm.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/node/farm.rs): `eligible` fails when this daemon does not host the goal, so the publisher suspends the page by today's rule. The delete-only path of `FarmOff` also serves an entry whose page this daemon published and no longer hosts.
- [node/flow.rs](../crates/locust-core/src/node/flow.rs): `drive_flow` also signs, where this daemon hosts, a `MemberRemoved` for each held set-aside removal signed by the key of an earlier term on the chain whose member is still active under the admission that removal names. It copies `last_accepted` and draws a new content key. It reads no level, like every automatic act.

**Exit criteria.**
- The three cargo commands, the four site commands and the two check scripts pass.

- A removes a member while B is stopped: `goal status` on A says B has not received 1 removal. B takes over without it; when A returns, B's `events` shows a second `member_removed` signed as host with no command run.
- `goal give` on A, `goal takeover` on B: `events` on every daemon shows no record of A's key after the base.

**Risks and notes.**
- A notice is one record. A computer that missed two changes learns only the first; that is enough for it to stop.
- A computer that is off is told when it is next on and someone who holds the record is too.
- A host that was replaced and has not learned it can still remove members; the new host's computer repeats those removals. A hostile host is not assumed.
- A removed member that no change concerns is still never told of its removal. That stays left out.
- Size, a judgement: 900 to 1,300 production lines and about 1,500 lines of tests.

### B3: Qualification and release

**Goal.** The finished behaviour is run on real daemons, the one sentence a person must understand is tested on people, and the release says what ends.

**Depends on.** B1 and B2.

**Changes.** No product code. Seven recipes, each with its expected output kept beside it under `research/`:
- A host on one machine is switched off; the backup on a second machine takes over; a third joins on a new ticket; the first machine returns.
- The same with the first machine asleep, not off, and admitting a joiner after it wakes.
- The host removes the backup, which takes over without having heard.
- The backup's data folder is put back from a copy made before its takeover, once with the marks kept and once with the whole home copied; it is host again without a second takeover.
- A takeover is made twice from two bases by overriding twice; status prints the conflict and the printed command settles it.
- A public goal: the page, the door and the gallery row after a takeover, on the new host and on the old.
- A home from protocol 7 started under 8.

**Tests.** None beyond those of B1 and B2.

**Exit criteria.**
- Every recipe passes on fresh homes on two machines. This is the first recorded run of Locust with sleep and wake between two machines.
- Five people who have not used Locust read the explanation and answer: what happens to someone the old host admitted last; what a host who was asleep finds; what wins if the host had removed the backup.
- The release notes, the site and operations.md carry the sentences of text B-9.

**Risks and notes.**
- The takeover of a present host cannot be tested for intent, only for outcome.

draft.safety:
Over held sets. Who hosts, the chain, every standing and the current content key are one function of the set of signed events a computer holds. Two computers that hold the same set compute the same answer, in any arrival order. No clock, timeout, arrival order or identifier comparison enters; the one comparison used is position in a signer's own log, which is signed.

Over deliveries. Let a computer hold a set in which change record c is in force, and let one more event arrive.
1. c is still in force, unless the event is one of four kinds: (a) a record of the previous term's key at a position after c's base that removes c's member or is a `BackupSet` naming anyone else or nobody; (b) a `TakeoverWithdrawn` signed by c's own key after c; (c) a second live change record of the same term, which makes the term disputed and puts nothing else in force; (d) an event that does (a), (b) or (c) to a change of an earlier term that c is built on.
2. No different change record of the same term comes into force while c is live. From c in force to another in force, c must first be void by (a) or (b).
3. While c is in force, no record of the previous key outside c's kept log is effective, whenever it was delivered, and no record anchored at or depending on such a record is effective or pending.
4. A second record of the previous key at any position at or below the base changes no standing.
5. A change record whose kept log holds an end is never in force. An end outside the kept log does not end the goal while the change is in force.
6. Only the member the old key named can produce a change record that any computer keeps or counts.

Exactly when a takeover a daemon treated as in force is undone: when that daemon comes to hold (a), (b) or (d). Under (c) it is suspended, not undone. Nothing else undoes it: not a fork of any earlier key, not any other late record of the old host, not a restart.

What an undo does. Every record of the void change's key and of every later term's key is set aside: the admissions (those members are not members), the removals (those members are members again), the rule and role changes, the plan and file recordings. Work anchored at those records is excluded; its authors' next records at kept anchors count. The old key is the last term's key again and its records after the base are effective again. Content keys opened under the void term stay on the computers that hold them.

What is not safe, and is said in the texts. A removal held only by a lost computer is lost. A takeover is not final while the old host's computer may return with a removal or un-naming of the backup. The daemon rules (hear from one other computer; the guard; never withdraw the last live change) are liveness aids and a modified daemon can skip them; validity does not rest on them.
draft.liveness:
Naming, changing and clearing the backup: only the host's computer must be on; one command each.

Taking over: the backup's computer must be on and its person runs one command and says yes. One other computer of the goal, not the old host's, must answer two exchanges, or there is no such computer, or the person adds `--alone`. The old host need not be reachable. A member's computer follows the new host as soon as it syncs with any computer that holds the record.

After a takeover: members fetch the new content key from the new host's computer or from any member that has it. The new host's computer must stay on for admissions and recordings, as the old one had to.

When the goal is stuck, and how it gets unstuck.
- No backup named and the host's computer lost: nobody joins or is removed and the rules never change; tasks, results and approvals go on. Nothing unsticks it. This is today's behaviour and the price of naming being optional.
- The backup's computer is lost too: the same.
- The backup's computer is catching up after a restore: it waits for its own records, or for `goal continue` (G2).
- No other computer answers: `--alone`.
- Two takeovers dispute a term: membership and rules are halted on every computer that holds both. The person who signed them runs the command status prints, from any copy of their data. Between two different backups the one who gives way runs it; if that person is gone it stays halted.
- The last term's governance log is forked (a restored host that continued): halted until that term's backup takes over from one branch; with none named, for good, as today.
- A takeover was voided by the old host's record: the old host hosts again and must be on. If that computer is then lost and it had named nobody else, the goal is stuck as in the first line.
- The current rules cannot be read after a takeover: the new host binds rules.
- A handoff that the other person never completes: the giver runs `goal keep`.

draft.model_first:
Two models under research/tla, written and run before chain.rs is touched, registered in research/tla/cases.json in the fast and extended suites and as the suite `hostchange`.

1. `HostChange.tla`, a replay model in the form of Organization.tla: a fixed signed transcript per scenario, TLC delivers it in every order with duplicates. It restates the governance projection with the signer as a function of position: governance keys 0 (first), 6, 7 and 8; agents 5 (the first host's), 1, 2, 3. Kinds: genesis, admit, remove, rules, backup, change, withdraw, end, a host step, and member work with an anchor and typed dependencies. A key epoch is a counter in the snapshot. Properties over held sets: `ReplayMatchesHeld`; `OneHostPerTerm`; `NothingAfterBase` (with a change in force no record of the previous key outside the kept log is in the view); `NoPendingFromSetAside`; `RevocationWins`; `EndRule`; `KeptLogIgnoresForks`; `EpochFollowsChain` (an effective record's epoch is the one at its anchor, and a change adds one). Properties over a delivery step, which no model has today: `UndoHasACause` (a change leaves force only on delivery of one of the four named kinds) and `NoSilentSwap` (no other change of the term enters force while the first is live). Scenarios, each with a config: one change; old-key records after the base delivered before and after; an old-key fork below the base, at the base and above it; a host step after the base and a decision after one predecessor by two keys; work anchored at a set-aside record followed by the same author at a kept anchor; a removal of the backup after the base; a rename with both the old and the new backup taking; a never-named member's change record; two changes on two bases of one branch, then a withdrawal; two changes on two branches of a forked log; an end at, before and after the base; a second and a third change, then the first one revoked; a change with its base withheld. Three mutations must each fail their property: revocation ignored, set aside judged by anchor in place of log position, kept log read as the usable prefix.

2. `HostChangeNodes.tla`, a small node model, because a restored honest daemon is a transition and not an assumption. Three computers (host, backup, one member), bounded logs. Actions: Sign, Name, Remove, Sync(a, b), Takeover(b) under the daemon rule, Alone, Copy, RestoreStore, RestoreAll, Continue, Withdraw, Give, Keep, Lose(host). Invariants: an ordinary start and a wake never block a takeover; a takeover repeated from the same base adds no record; no reachable state without Continue or Alone has two live changes. Named traces kept as witnesses: a removed backup taking over from before its removal, then the removal delivered; a restored backup with the marks kept recomputing its key; a restored backup with the marks lost taking over from another base, then the withdrawal; a host asleep admitting after the base; a handoff with nothing set aside; and, left open on purpose, a removal held only by the lost host.

Also before building: two cases in Workspace.tla (an old-key acceptance after the base is not selected; a new-key acceptance after the same predecessor as a kept old-key one is disputed) and one in FlowEffects.tla (a set-aside stage step never defines a task's round).

Not modelled, and said so in the model's page: `screen` and retention (convergence of what is held is argued in prose and pinned by the Rust test on screen); the notice route; the content of keys; that the Rust code refines the model.

When the new host's computer later receives a removal the old host had signed, should it repeat that removal by itself? Recommended: yes. Otherwise a removed stranger reads the goal until the new host acts. The cost: a host that has been replaced and does not know it yet can still remove members.

Roles that only the old host's agent held pass to the new host's agent at a takeover. Accept? Recommended: yes; otherwise a goal with a lead has nobody who can pick or close until the new host runs one command per role.
A takeover with no other member's computer heard from is refused unless the person adds `--alone`. Accept? Recommended: yes. It is what stops a backup that was removed and never told.

After a takeover the public page gets a new address, every member consents again, and the old page of a lost host keeps its last content until the farm service expires it. Accept for this version? Recommended: yes; moving a page to a new key needs the service to read the signed history and is a later step.

If the old host's own history was forked by a restore and named a different backup on each side, and both take over, one of them must withdraw. If that person is gone, members and rules stay frozen. Accept as a stated limit? Recommended: accept; it takes four faults.

Do you want `goal give` and `goal keep`, or is it enough that a host names the other person and that person takes over? Recommended: keep the two commands; with them a handoff drops nothing, without them an admission in the last second can be dropped.

A named backup can take over while the host's computer is on and reachable; the plan says so and does not refuse. This follows your answer that the backup can take over alone. Confirm? Recommended: yes.

The un-naming rule is by position: any record of the old host after the point the backup continued from that names another backup, or nobody, or removes the backup, voids the takeover, with everything done since. That can arrive long after. Should the new host's status keep one line until the old host's computer has been heard from? Recommended: yes, one line of fact on the new host's computer only.

On a home from before version 8, should Locust 8 refuse to start and print where the old goals are, or move the old folder aside by itself? Recommended: refuse and print; moving a person's data unasked is not ours to do.
Are the words right: backup host, take over, hand over, dropped?

unsure: Nothing was built or run. K1, G1, G2, E1 to E3 and R1 to R10 are plan text; every function, field and test name taken from them may differ on the tree B1 lands on, and B1 must be read again against that tree.

That an Ed25519 signature made by this code is the same on every run. crypto.rs calls the library's plain `sign`, which is deterministic by its standard; I did not check the pinned library version or run it. Byte-identical repeat rests on it.

That ordinary sync carries every held author's records, a governance key's included, to every member. I read the responder and the driver, not the initiator and the outbox; K1's check says the sync code filters no author by membership.

`screen` for a change record is a cheap test (base held, endorser once named). A member that was once named can make daemons that do not yet hold its un-naming store change records that will never count. Each is one author in every frontier, which holds 4,096. I bound this by the fault model (a named party is honest), not by a rule.

Revocation by position in place of descent. It is what lets one record prove a void takeover to a computer that is no longer a member. On an old log forked by a restore it can void a takeover because of a record on the other branch. I think that matches the owner's intent (the host's un-naming wins) but it was not checked by a model.
Whether copying `last_accepted` from a set-aside removal always passes the cutoff check in `Chain::cutoff` on the new chain. It should, because the admission id is the same; not run.

During a dispute, records after the common kept log read as after a halt and work anchored there waits, as under today's fork. That is the one place a record waits because of a change of host. I chose it because nothing is decided yet; the model property about pending is stated for set-aside records only.
Passing sole-held roles to the new host's agent treats a list of exactly the old host's agent as the fallback. A host who gave itself a role on purpose loses it at a takeover.

The new host's status line about finality needs to know that the old host's computer was heard from after the takeover. I gave it a local record of when the takeover was signed and today's last-sync time per computer; this is display only.

The base on a forked old log is chosen by the taker's daemon (the branch with more records, or `--base`). That is a local choice shown in the plan, not something computers must agree on; the wording of that plan line is not written.
The evidence exchange's frame limit today is two headers. A notice is one, so it fits; I did not read the shell code that applies the limit.

A daemon that held a set-aside record's content key can read that text locally by trying the keys it holds for the blob's epoch number. I did not design how an author is shown that text for reposting.
Whether `goal give` and `goal keep` earn their place. They are in B2 so that B1 stands without them.
Every size is a judgement. The reviewers of the earlier round put this family at 4,000 to 6,000 lines; my figure for B1 and B2 together is inside that.

attack.verdict:
Not sound as written. I found 2 fatal breaks, 7 serious ones and 4 minor ones. The validity rule itself (who hosts, as a function of the held set) held up against every forgery I tried. The breaks are in the parts the design chose not to model: what a computer keeps (`screen`), the notice route, the automatic repeat of removals, the daemon rules around a restore, and the command checks. Both fatal breaks come from one sentence in B1 ("A `HostChanged` that a held record already revokes is dropped") and from the notice rule choosing recipients by the sender's own view of who is a member.

Read in the code (tree at 43f03b4): crates/locust-core/src/goal/chain.rs (whole: `Chain::build`, `traverse_cutoff`, `authorize`, the ancestry walk), history.rs, screen.rs, mod.rs (`Goal::next`), fold.rs (`decision`, the successor index, `current_round`), standing.rs; node/peers.rs, replica.rs, commit.rs (`advance`), authoring.rs, entry.rs, requests/goals.rs, farm.rs (`eligible`); sync/responder.rs, driver.rs, the first 200 lines of initiator.rs; locust-proto event.rs (`Body`, `dependencies`), seal.rs (layout and construction), sync.rs and limits.rs for the frontier cap. Read in plans and notes: the master plan, the whole replacement note, both characterization notes, finding 12, the three safety pieces' summaries, plugs and the 28 seams, G1's text in full, the first part of roles Phase 8. Inferred, not run: every behaviour after B1 and B2, and every sequence below, which are hand traces of the design's rules over the code as read. K1, G1, G2, E1 and R1 to R10 are plan text.

breaks.claim: Two hosts that never converge. The host's removal of the backup cannot surface once the new host has removed the old host's agent, or once a removed backup took over with --alone. Decision 18 then never applies.
breaks.steps:
1. A, B, C hold g0..g6. g6 = BackupSet(Juniper).
2. Ana runs `member remove` for Juniper: g7 by G0 at position 7. It reaches nobody. A sleeps.
3. Ben runs `goal takeover`. C is heard from. T = HostChanged(base (6,g6), host Juniper) by K1. B and C compute: T in force.
4. Ben runs `member remove` for Harbor: h1 by K1. The design allows it (test `the_old_hosts_agent_can_be_removed_after_a_change_and_the_new_one_cannot`). B and C: Harbor is no member.
5. A wakes. A computes chain g0..g7, host Ana, Juniper removed. A dials C, because Maple is a member for A. C answers NotAMember: for C, A's endpoint is bound to no member, and an unadmitted exchange serves only Join and a proof (read: responder.rs). A does not dial B.
6. C and B push T to A as a notice (B2: an endpoint named in an admission and bound to no current member). A's `screen` drops it: a held record, g7, already revokes it. C and B write record `n` and never send it again.
7. A's `evidence()` is empty: it holds no change record. Nothing carries g7 to B or C.
Result. A: host Ana, members Harbor, Maple, Wren; it admits Dee on an old ticket and records plan and file changes. B and C: host Ben, members Juniper, Maple, Wren. No computer ever holds both g7 and T.
Variant, B1's own second exit drill: g7 reached C before A stopped. B takes over with --alone. C refuses B on every dial, so T reaches nobody. Nobody holds T, so nobody sends g7 to B. B believes it hosts for good and admits joiners. The drill's expected result (all three show Ana as host) cannot happen.
Variant with `screen` repaired but B lost after step 4: A keeps T as void and pushes g7 only to endpoints that are non-members in A's view. That is B alone. C and W refuse A and are never sent g7.
breaks.fix: Three small changes. (a) Never drop a void change record at receipt. (b) Make the evidence exchange answer: a computer that receives a change record for which it holds a voiding record sends that record back in the same exchange. (c) A daemon that is refused NotAMember by an endpoint it counts as a member's sends that endpoint, on the evidence exchange, the change record it treats as in force, or the voiding record it holds. Then model it: add to HostChangeNodes the actions RemoveOldHostsAgent and Notice, and the property that two honest computers that can reach each other end with the same host.

breaks.claim: The accepted undo case itself (S4a) strands every member who worked under the void term, on the host's computer and on every computer that learned the removal first. The outcome depends on arrival order.
breaks.steps:
1. S4a as written, up to: A wakes holding g7 and syncs with C.
2. C sends T, h1, h2, s3 and Maple's m1 (anchor h2). A's `screen` drops T, because held g7 revokes it. It then drops h1, h2, s3: K1 is not the governance key of any held change record. It keeps m1: Maple was admitted by G0.
3. On A, m1's anchor h2 is not held. Today's rule gives Pending(Anchor) (read: `authorize_base`). The design's new rule covers only an anchor that is held and set aside.
4. Maple posts m2 anchored at g7. On C, which held T before g7: h2 is held and set aside, m1 is skipped, m2 is Effective. On A: the walk from m2 reaches m1, whose anchor has no position, so m2 is Pending(Anchor). So is every later record of Maple, for good. A can never keep h2.
5. A is the host. Its daemon records nothing that rests on Maple's work. A and C hold different sets for ever and compute different standings.
The same happens on any member's computer that received g7 before T. S4a's own text ("A gets T, h1, h2, s3", "A's status lists what Juniper did that is dropped", text B-6) contradicts the screen sentence in B1: A holds none of it.
breaks.fix: Screen keeps a change record whenever its kept log is held and the record is authorized there, void or not. Its key's records are then kept and judged set aside on every computer. If the kept log is not yet held, drop and let the next exchange bring it again. Bound the count per (named member, term) instead of dropping void ones. S4b's sentence becomes: C keeps T as void.

breaks.claim: The automatic repeat of an old host's removal undoes more than the design says. It can wipe a member's whole history, retract work that counted under the new host, and remove the new host's own named backup, which can void the next takeover with no person deciding.
breaks.steps:
Cutoff that does not validate:
1. Base g6. A signs g7 = admits X. Wren, synced with A, posts w3 anchored at g7. A signs g8 = MemberRemoved(Wren, g5, last_accepted w3). A is lost.
2. B takes over from g6. Later it receives g7, g8, w3. Its daemon signs h1 = MemberRemoved(Wren, g5, w3), unasked.
3. Every computer runs `traverse_cutoff` on h1. The cutoff record w3 has anchor g7, which is set aside and has no snapshot. `tenure_at` answers none, so the function returns the empty set (read: chain.rs). Every record Wren ever signed under admission g5 is PastRemoval, months of kept work included, and so is whatever rested on it. On a computer that lacks w3, all of Wren's records are Pending(Reference) instead.
Work that counted:
4. In S6 case 2 Wren is a member for two days. Wren approves Maple's change; B's daemon records it. The repeat with cutoff w3 makes that approval PastRemoval. The cutoff test runs before any pin (read: `authorize_base`), so the recorded acceptance loses its evidence and the files head moves back.

breaks.claim: A takeover never becomes final, although the design says it is final once the old host's computer is heard from. A host that already accepted the change voids it months later after a restore. A removed hostile member can void it at will through the notice route, re-enter, and leave the survivors unable to write text.

Restored old host:
1. g6 = BackupSet(Juniper). T, base (6,g6). A receives T and stops signing with G0; G0's mark is (6,g6). Three months pass. T2 and T3 follow.
2. A's data folder is put back from a copy made before A received T. Marks kept. G0's mark equals the store's tip, so G0 is not behind and is not held (G1: every other key signs at once). On A, T is not held and Ana is host.
3. Before A's first exchange Ana runs `backup clear`: g7 by G0 at position 7.
4. A syncs. Everywhere: g7 is a G0 record after base 6 that names nobody. T is revoked, T2 and T3 are not in force, G0 is the last term. Three months of admissions, removals, rules and recordings are set aside. This is not decision 18: the host had heard.
Withheld record:
5. g6 = BackupSet(Juniper). Ana removes Juniper: g7, epoch 1, key k1. Record and key reach only M, a hostile member. A is lost for good.
6. B hears from C and takes over. Later Ben removes M (h5).
7. Months later M sends g7 to B and C as a notice. `receive_notice` keeps it: M's endpoint is in an old admission, and g7 is a removal by a known governance key that voids a held change record.
8. B and C: T revoked. Chain g0..g7: host Ana, who is lost; no backup; M a member again, because h5 is set aside; epoch 1 under k1, which only M holds. No honest computer can write text (measured today for a removal whose key did not arrive). Nobody can take over. The liveness section says tasks, results and approvals go on in this state. breaks.fix: Guard: after any found restore, a governance key this daemon holds signs nothing until one other computer of the goal has been heard from, also when the key is not behind. For finality, one record: the old host's daemon, on holding a live change of its term and no record that voids it, signs `HostYielded { change }` with the old key by itself; a change is not revoked by an old-key record at a position at or after a held yield. The yield also puts a mark ahead of any older copy, so G1 holds a restored old host. Steps 5 to 8 remain whenever the old host never returns: say so in the texts, correct the liveness line, and ask the owner whether decision 18 has an end.

1. S3: T, base (7,s7), key K1. B signs h1..h43. C holds them. Ben named Maple backup at h5.
2. B's whole computer is restored from a copy whose tip is s7. Marks lost. Nobody reachable. Ben runs `goal continue`, then `goal takeover --alone`. The daemon signs the same bytes T.
3. B's daemon now hosts. Its first unattended act (a plan recording, an admission on a new ticket, a repeated removal) is signed by K1 at position 1: h1' differs from h1. Nothing stops it: the guard was continued, K1 has no mark, nobody was heard.

With a random key this was a dispute Ben could settle with one command.
